summary: Runs and maintains gantry or robotic-arm printers (e.g. ICON Vulcan, COBOD BOD2, Apis Cor) that extrude cementitious mix to build walls for homes, barracks and small structures, and handles mix QC, print logs and inspection paperwork under codes still forming (IRC Appendix AW, UL 3401, ICC-ES AC509). AI helps most with turning print and test data into troubleshooting plans, daily logs, inspector-ready documentation, and learning a fast-moving standards landscape.

prompts.title: Pre-print readiness checklist
prompts.task: Build a site-specific checklist before starting a wall print
prompts.prompt: You are a senior 3D construction printing site lead. Build a pre-print readiness checklist for tomorrow's print on [PROJECT/ADDRESS] using a [PRINTER MODEL, e.g. COBOD BOD2 / ICON Vulcan] with [MIX NAME/SUPPLIER]. Forecast: [TEMP RANGE, HUMIDITY, WIND, RAIN CHANCE]. Wall plan: [WALL HEIGHT, LAYER HEIGHT, BEAD WIDTH, PLANNED LAYERS PER DAY]. Cover: gantry/rail level and calibration, pump and hose inspection, mix batching and fresh-property checks (flow, set time), weather protection and curing, reinforcement and embed placement points, crew roles, and stop-work triggers. Output as a table: Item | Check method | Acceptance criterion | Owner | Done. Mark any criterion you are assuming rather than taking from the manufacturer's or engineer's documents.
prompts.caution: Acceptance criteria must come from the printer manufacturer, mix supplier and engineer of record, not from Claude's defaults.

prompts.title: Layer defect troubleshooting
prompts.task: Diagnose cold joints, slumping, tearing or cracking in printed layers
prompts.prompt: Act as a materials and process troubleshooter for extrusion-based concrete printing. During today's print we saw [DEFECT: e.g. layer slumping after layer 12 / bead tearing / cold joints / plastic shrinkage cracks] on [WALL SEGMENT]. Conditions: ambient [TEMP], mix temp [TEMP], time between layers [MINUTES], pump pressure [VALUE], print speed [VALUE], flow table result [VALUE], water added on site [YES/NO, AMOUNT]. Give a ranked list of likely causes (buildability, open time, interlayer interval, nozzle standoff, mix variability), the evidence that would confirm or rule out each, and corrective actions for the next print. Then state whether the affected section likely needs engineer review before more layers go on.
prompts.caution: Structural acceptance of a defective section is the engineer of record's call, not the technician's or Claude's.

prompts.title: Daily print log
prompts.task: Turn raw notes and printer logs into a clean daily construction log
prompts.prompt: You are documenting a 3D-printed construction project for the owner, engineer and building inspector. Convert my raw notes and printer data into a daily print log. Inputs: [PASTE NOTES, PRINTER LOG EXCERPT, BATCH TICKETS, TEST RESULTS, PHOTOS LIST]. Format: header (date, project, permit no. [NUMBER], crew, weather), print summary (walls/segments, layers completed, start/stop times, interruptions and why), material log (batches, lot numbers, fresh tests, specimens cast for [ASTM C109 cubes / C39 cylinders]), deviations from print plan, safety observations, and open items. Keep it factual; flag any gaps in the data rather than filling them in.
prompts.caution: Never invent test values or batch numbers; the log may become part of the permit and warranty record.

prompts.title: Inspector submittal package
prompts.task: Prepare documentation for a building inspection of printed walls
prompts.prompt: Help me prepare for a building inspection of 3D-printed walls in [JURISDICTION]. The jurisdiction has adopted [IRC EDITION / LOCAL AMENDMENTS] and the system has [EVALUATION REPORT, e.g. ICC-ES report number, or 'none']. Using these documents [PASTE OR SUMMARIZE: engineering drawings, mix design, test results, print logs], produce: 1) a checklist of what an inspector is likely to request (e.g. evidence of compliance with IRC Appendix AW / UL 3401, compressive strength data, reinforcement and embed locations, wall dimensions vs. plans), 2) which items I have and which are missing, 3) a short cover memo. Flag where the code path in my jurisdiction is unclear and should be confirmed with the building official.
prompts.caution: Code adoption varies by jurisdiction; confirm requirements with the building official and the engineer of record.

prompts.title: Explaining printed homes to neighbors or buyers
prompts.task: Write plain-language public communication about a printed build
prompts.prompt: You are a communications lead for a 3D-printed housing builder. Write a one-page plain-language FAQ for [AUDIENCE: neighbors / home buyers / city council] about the printed homes at [PROJECT]. Address: what is printed vs. conventionally built (roof, windows, MEP), how strength and durability are tested, fire and weather performance as supported by [OUR TEST DATA / EVALUATION REPORT], noise and hours of printing, insurance and resale questions, and what is still unknown about long-term performance. Tone: honest, no hype, 8th-grade reading level. Mark any claim I need to verify with our engineering team.
prompts.caution: Don't make durability, fire or cost claims beyond what test data and listings support.

prompts.title: Print schedule and weather plan
prompts.task: Plan a multi-day print sequence around weather and cure times
prompts.prompt: Act as a construction planner for a 3D concrete printing crew. Plan the print sequence for [NUMBER] walls / [TOTAL LINEAR FT] on [PROJECT] over [DATE RANGE]. Constraints: printer throughput [VALUE], max layers per session per engineer [VALUE], mix working temp range [RANGE], forecast [PASTE], crew availability [DETAILS], embed/rebar/window buck installs at layers [LIST], and inspection hold points [LIST]. Output a day-by-day table (date, segments, layers, crew, hold points, weather risk, backup plan) plus a list of critical-path risks. Note any assumptions about cure time or hot/cold-weather practice (e.g. ACI 305/306) that need confirmation.
prompts.caution: Treat Claude's schedule as a draft; cure and loading limits come from the engineer and mix supplier.

prompts.title: Job hazard analysis
prompts.task: Draft a JHA for printer setup, printing and teardown
prompts.prompt: You are a construction safety specialist familiar with OSHA 29 CFR 1926. Draft a job hazard analysis for [TASK: gantry assembly / printing / pump cleanout / teardown] with a [PRINTER TYPE] on [SITE CONDITIONS]. Include hazards such as moving gantry and pinch points, pressurized hose and pump line blockages, silica and cement exposure, skin burns from wet cement, working at height on the gantry, lifting and rigging, heat stress, and lockout/tagout during maintenance. Output: Step | Hazard | Controls (elimination to PPE) | Responsible person. End with items needing the competent person's or manufacturer's input.
prompts.caution: A JHA must be reviewed by the site's competent person and match the manufacturer's safety manual.

prompts.title: Upskilling study plan
prompts.task: Learn the materials science, standards and equipment behind the job
prompts.prompt: I am a [CURRENT BACKGROUND, e.g. concrete finisher / CNC machinist / new grad] moving into 3D construction printing with [EMPLOYER TYPE]. Build me a 12-week study plan covering: rheology and buildability of printable mortars, testing (ASTM C1437 flow, C109/C39 strength, interlayer bond), reinforcement strategies, the standards landscape (IRC Appendix AW, UL 3401, ICC-ES AC509, ISO/ASTM 52939), printer kinematics and slicing, and site safety. For each week: key concepts, 2-3 resources by type (standards body, peer-reviewed review papers, manufacturer training), and a hands-on exercise. Mark which standards are still evolving and where I should verify the current edition.
prompts.caution: Claude may misremember standard editions or numbers; check the issuing body's website for the current version.
